new_en: (32) "He poured water," etc. This refers to one who poured only the first waters, using part of a revi'it on 1 hand, and then rubbed it with the second hand, which had not been washed, because he thought that this rubbing would count as washing the second hand as well. The same law applies if the rubbing was done merely to remove sweat or dirt, or if there was simply incidental contact. (33) "It did not count," etc. It did not count for the second hand, and the first hand also became impure through contact with the other hand, as explained below. (34) "They became impure." The first waters are considered impure because they became impure through contact with the hand during washing, as explained above in seif 2. (35) "And when he rubbed it, it became impure," etc. This new impurity is more severe than a case in which the hands had not been washed at all. Water that became impure on the hand from this external contact will not be purified even if many kavim of water are poured over it, until the hand is first dried. So explains the Rosh. (36) "The other hand." Consequently the first hand itself also became impure, and it too must be dried, because its water received impurity through contact with the second, impure hand. Second waters purify only the impurity originating in the hand itself; they do not purify impurity that came upon the water from another source. Accordingly, if one poured first waters separately over both hands and then rubbed the hands together, the waters on the hands make each other impure and second waters do not suffice to purify them, as explained below in seif 6. (37) "Therefore one who pours," etc. Since the other hand became impure and thereby the first hand became impure as well, he must first dry both hands and then wash them again properly. Without drying, repeated pouring is ineffective. (38) "Therefore one who washes," etc. Since one must be careful that 1 hand not touch the other before the washing is complete, and this is a common source of error, it is preferable to use 1 of 3 methods: another person pours a revi'it over both hands at once; he does this himself in the manner explained below; or he pours a revi'it at once over each hand separately. In these ways the hands become completely pure, and afterward their touching each other causes no problem. On the contrary, it is a mitzvah initially to rub them together. (39) "Upon them." Meaning upon both hands at once. They are then considered like 1 hand and do not become impure by touching each other during the washing, as explained below in seif 5. (40) "And if he has no other person," etc. When another person is available, it is preferable that the other person pour, because when he washes by himself while holding the vessel with his fingertips, it is difficult to ensure that the water reaches the hands and the fingertips properly. (41) "Upon both hands at once." In this manner 1 revi'it is sufficient, and second waters are not needed. (42) "Or he should pour a revi'it on each one." Meaning that he should hold the vessel normally and pour a revi'it at once upon each hand separately. If he pours a revi'it only on 1 hand, that hand can become impure by touching the other. (43) "And afterward he rubs them." This applies to all the methods just mentioned. In each of them there is no longer any concern that rubbing will cause impurity. (44) "For the one who pours," etc. Meaning that through this method the purification of the hands is complete, and there is no longer any concern from their touching each other. (45) "If another person touched them." Even if he had already washed with second waters, or poured a revi'it at once so that his hands were completely purified, if another person whose hands were not washed touched them, he must dry his hands and wash them again.

In Taz, seif katan 7, "after he rubbed," etc. His words show that he explains the Shulchan Aruch's statement, "although so long as he has not rubbed, they are purified through rubbing," as follows. The difficulty is why this contact should render the hand impure, since there is a means of purification through the second waters together with rubbing. Taz answers that because the new contact occurred after the rubbing, the situation is worse. This is also clear from his later words, where he questions Levush: what was Levush's difficulty, when R' Shimshon and the Shulchan Aruch explicitly teach that rubbing can worsen the situation?

If the rubbing itself were what purified the water, why would rubbing a second time not help after the hand was touched again? The same type of impure water was previously on the hand and the hands were purified through rubbing. Even now, after renewed contact, one could seemingly rub again. This is the meaning of the phrase that he "returned and touched," and the matter is straightforward in light of Magen Avraham, seif katan 16.

Taz, seif katan 16, cites Maharshal as requiring rubbing in every case, and one might wish to prove from there that the second waters do not purify until rubbing. This is not correct. Mishbetzot Zahav explains that Maharshal means that even after second waters, drying remains necessary because of the rule that one who eats without drying his hands is treated as though he ate impure bread. The second waters certainly purify the first waters. The hands nevertheless require proper drying. This is also the intent of R' Shimshon.
In chapter 1 of Yadayim, according to the explanation of the Tosefta cited by the Rosh.

Seif katan 10, "upon the second." "And if he touched," etc., "he need not dry them," etc., because they had already become pure. Yam Shel Shlomo explains that the rule in seif 4 is different. There, when only first waters had been poured and the hand touched the other, unwashed hand, those waters then contained 2 forms of impurity: first, the ordinary impurity of first waters that results from washing the hand; second, the additional impurity that came from contact with the other impure hand. When he washes the first hand a second time, the second waters cannot purify 2 separate forms of impurity, for we find that second waters purify only 1 type of impurity, namely the impurity the water received from the hand that was washed.

Here, however, where a revi'it was poured or the first hand had already been washed twice and its water had become pure, contact with the second hand introduces only 1 new form of impurity. Therefore another proper washing can purify it. This is the distinction underlying the Shulchan Aruch's rulings.

If another person's impure hand touched the water, the rules explained above apply. Where drying is required, he must first dry and then wash again. I had difficulty with the wording cited in the previous seif katan concerning grasping the vessel, because when one pours a revi'it over the hand, the hand is already pure. If he then touches the vessel and later touches it again, the analysis depends upon whether actual impure water was transferred back to the hand. Similarly, when he holds the vessel by its handle with his second hand before that hand has been washed, this alone does not render the water impure, because the water does not become impure merely through the impure hand's contact with the outside of the vessel, as explained here.

"The bread." If it has a handle-like projection, it should be removed. Hagahot Minhagim. When he says the Divine Name he should raise the bread, and on Shabbos he raises both loaves. Maharil; Magen Avraham. "With bread." These are: "You shall not plow with an ox and donkey together," kilayim, leket, shikhechah, peah, bikkurim, terumat maaser, maaser sheni, and challah.

"And he may not recite the blessing," etc. The explanation is that we rule that with all blessings, once a person has fulfilled his own obligation he may nevertheless discharge the obligation of others, except for blessings over enjoyment. If he already fulfilled such a blessing, he may not recite it merely for others. Therefore, regarding HaMotzi over matzah and Borei Pri HaGafen over the wine of Kiddush, these are not treated simply as blessings over enjoyment, because there is a mitzvah incumbent upon him. He may therefore discharge others even when he does not taste together with them. The bread of Shabbos is different. Although there is an obligation to eat it, the blessing remains a blessing over enjoyment, and one who is not eating may not discharge others. The reason appears to be that bread is a person's principal ordinary food and eating bread is not uniquely an act of mitzvah, since he eats bread on weekdays as well. Matzah and the wine of Kiddush are different because there is a special change in their use at that time.

"From which he broke." Bach writes that the portion of bread upon which the mitzvah was performed should be treated with special respect and should not be fed to an animal, bird, or other inappropriate recipient. The portion should be consumed in a respectful manner by one for whom it is fitting. I have seen many who are careful with remnants of bread used for a mitzvah in this way. I brought a further proof in my work on Rashi, Parashat Bo, regarding the verse, "their kneading bowls bound in their garments," etc., that there is an expression of cherishing a mitzvah in what remains from matzah and maror.

Pat haba'ah b'kisnin: Some explain that this means bread made in the form of pockets that are filled with honey or sugar, walnuts, almonds, and spices, which are called rusklayish and dialchashu. Others say that it is dough into which honey, oil, milk, or various spices were mixed and which was then baked, provided that the taste of the fruit juice or spices is perceptible in the dough. Some say that this is nevertheless considered ordinary bread unless it contains a large quantity of spices or honey, as in types of cake called lekach, where the honey and spices are nearly the principal ingredients, and this is the custom. [Rashi; Aruch; Rambam can also be understood this way.] Others explain that it means bread, whether spiced or unspiced, made into dry cakes that are chewed, which are called biskunis. The halacha follows all these views, and all of these foods are governed by the laws stated regarding pat haba'ah b'kisnin.

Chalut, meaning a kind of bread that is scalded in boiling water, which was afterward baked in an oven, is complete bread, and one recites HaMotzi over it. {Rama: Likewise, something made from a soft batter that was baked in an oven without liquid has the law of bread, and one recites HaMotzi and the 3 blessings of Birkat HaMazon over it. The same applies if it was baked in a pot without liquid. [Tosafos; Rosh; Ran, chapter Kol Sha'ah; Rambam, chapter 6 of Hilchot Challah; She'iltot; Tur] A small amount of liquid used merely to grease the pot so that the dough will not burn is not considered liquid. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 3 of Hilchot Berachos] But something made from a soft batter and fried in liquid is, according to all opinions, not bread. [Tosafos; Rosh; Ran; Rabbeinu Yonah, chapter Keitzad Mevarchin]}

Seif katan 3, "and women," etc. The wording begins with 2 categories, saying that women and servants should not say "covenant" and "Torah." This implies that women should say neither covenant nor Torah, and servants likewise should say neither. Yet it concludes with only 1 reason, that women are not members of the covenant, which would imply that women may say Torah and that servants may say covenant.

Tosafos at the beginning of Perek Mi SheMeito, Berachos 20b, explain the question whether women's obligation in Birkat HaMazon is rabbinic on the ground that they are not included equally in covenant and Torah; this was cited above in siman 185. In Berachos 49a, Rabbi Zeira said to Rav Chisda, "Let the master come and teach." Rav Chisda replied that he had not mastered Birkat HaMazon. The Gemara's discussion indicates that omission of covenant and Torah is significant where the wording must be suitable for all those being discharged.

The difficulty remains concerning the wording for women and servants. If the reason regarding Torah were simply that women do not study the entire Torah, one must still account for the fact that women recite Birkat HaTorah because they are obligated to learn the laws of the mitzvot that apply to them, as explained in siman 47 and Yoreh De'ah siman 246, seif 6. The verse "Thus shall you say to the house of Yaakov" is interpreted as referring to the women. Why, then, should they not say "Your Torah that You taught us"?

Likewise, Avodah Zarah 27a discusses whether a woman has the halachic status associated with brit milah. According to the derivation from "he shall surely perform the milah," a woman is regarded as included in that status, whereas according to the derivation from "and you shall keep My covenant," women are not members of that covenant. It is therefore possible that women may say the wording, "Your covenant that You sealed in our flesh," according to the first approach, because they are treated as belonging to the covenantal category.

When Rav Chisda omitted covenant and Torah in a zimun that discharged women, the point was that those phrases do not apply to women in precisely the same manner as to men. Men bear the actual sign of brit milah and are commanded in study of the entire Torah. This explains the view that if covenant and Torah were omitted from Birkat HaMazon one nevertheless fulfilled the obligation.

Regarding pronunciation: the wording should be read carefully in "lo chiser lanu" and "al yechsar lanu," with the vocalization recorded by the authorities. "She'atah zan" likewise has its proper vocalization, and "b'fi kol chai" is read as a construct phrase; see siman 51. Shelah writes that one should say "chaser yechsar," and explains that the numerical value represented by the vowels corresponds to "lechem."
